note: mœurs: pliant customs of a people
replacement: As long as family feeling was alive, the man who opposed oppression was never alone. He looked around him and found his clients, his hereditary friends, and his relatives. If this support was lacking, his ancestors sustained him and his descendants inspired him. But when inherited estates are divided, and a few years are enough to blur the distinctions of a race, where can family feeling be found? What force can there be in the customs of a country that has changed and is still constantly changing its face? In such a country every act of tyranny has a precedent and every crime an example. Nothing is so old that its age can save it from destruction, and nothing so unheard of that its novelty can prevent it from being done. What resistance can customs offer when they are so pliant that they have already often given way? What strength can even public opinion have kept, when no twenty persons are connected by a common tie? When not a single man, family, chartered corporation, class, or free institution has the power to represent or assert that opinion? When every citizen, equally weak, equally poor, and equally dependent, has only his personal helplessness to set against the organized force of the government?

The annals of France offer nothing like the condition into which that country might then be thrown. It is better compared to the times of old, to those hideous eras of Roman oppression, when the customs of the people were corrupted, their traditions wiped out, their habits destroyed, and their opinions shaken. Freedom, driven out of the laws, could find no refuge in the land. Nothing protected the citizens, and the citizens no longer protected themselves. Human nature was the plaything of man, and princes wore out the mercy of Heaven before they exhausted the patience of their subjects. Those who hope to revive the monarchy of Henry IV or of Louis XIV seem to me to be afflicted with mental blindness. When I consider the present condition of several European nations, a condition toward which all the others are tending, I am led to believe that they will soon be left with no other alternative than democratic liberty or the tyranny of the Caesars. *n

And indeed it deserves consideration whether men are to be entirely emancipated or entirely enslaved, whether their rights are to be made equal or wholly taken away from them. Suppose the rulers of society were reduced either to raising the crowd gradually to their own level or to pushing the citizens below the level of humanity. Would not the doubts of many be resolved, the consciences of many be healed, and the community be prepared to make great sacrifices with little difficulty? In that case, the gradual growth of democratic customs and institutions should be regarded not as the best means of preserving freedom but as the only one. Even without liking democratic government, one might adopt it as the most workable and the fairest remedy for the present ills of society.

note: mœurs of a people, with laws
replacement: Anyone who, after reading this book, imagines that I wrote it to hold up the laws and customs of the Anglo-Americans as a model for all democratic peoples would be making a very great mistake. Such a reader must have paid more attention to the form of my ideas than to their substance. My aim has been to show, by the example of America, that there may be laws, and especially customs, that allow a democratic people to remain free. But I am very far from thinking that we should follow the example of the American democracy and copy the means it has used to reach its ends. I am well aware of the influence that the nature of a country and its political precedents have on a constitution, and I would regard it as a great misfortune for mankind if liberty were to exist all over the world in the same forms.

note: inside a quotation; kept as served
mœurs listed with customs and laws; mores avoids redundancy
replacement: As castes disappear and the classes of society draw closer together, as mores, customs, and laws change through the tumultuous contact of people with one another, as new facts arise, as new truths come to light, as ancient opinions fade and others take their place, the image of an ideal perfection, always on the wing, presents itself to the human mind. Continual changes then occur at every moment under everyone’s eyes. The position of some is made worse, and he learns only too well that no people and no individual, however enlightened, can claim to be infallible. The condition of others is improved, and from this he infers that man is endowed with an indefinite capacity for improvement. His setbacks teach him that no one may hope to have found absolute good; his successes spur him to pursue it without end. Thus, always seeking, always falling to rise again, often disappointed but not discouraged, he moves unceasingly toward that immeasurable greatness, so dimly visible at the end of the long road that humanity has yet to travel. It is hard to believe how many facts flow naturally from the philosophical theory of the indefinite perfectibility of man, or how strong an influence it has even on people who live entirely for action and not for thought, and who seem to conform their actions to it without knowing anything about it. I stop an American sailor and ask why the ships of his country are built to last such a short time. He answers without hesitation that the art of navigation is making such rapid progress every day that the finest vessel would become almost useless if it lasted beyond a certain number of years. In these words, which fell by chance and on a particular subject from a man of rough education, I recognize the general and systematic idea on which a great people directs all its affairs.

note: customs of antiquity shown on stage
replacement: When the heroes and customs of antiquity are often brought onto the stage, and playwrights faithfully follow the rules of old precedent, that is enough to conclude that the democratic classes have not yet gained the upper hand in the theaters. In the preface to “Britannicus,” Racine very humbly apologizes for having placed Junia among the Vestals, who, according to Aulus Gellius, he says, “admitted no one below six years of age nor above ten.” We may be sure he would neither have accused himself of this offense nor defended himself against criticism if he had been writing for our contemporaries. A fact of this kind shows the state of literature at the time, and it shows the state of society itself as well. A democratic stage does not prove that the nation is in a state of democracy, because, as we have just seen, even in aristocracies democratic tastes may influence the drama. But when the spirit of aristocracy reigns exclusively on the stage, that fact proves beyond refutation that the whole of society is aristocratic. One may boldly infer that the same lettered and learned class that sways the playwrights also commands the people and governs the country.

The refined tastes and arrogant bearing of an aristocracy will rarely fail to lead it, when it controls the stage, to make a kind of selection within human nature. Some conditions of society hold its chief interest, and the scenes that depict their customs are preferred on the stage. Certain virtues, and even certain vices, are thought to deserve a place there more than others, and these are applauded while all the rest are shut out. On the stage as elsewhere, an aristocratic audience wants to meet only people of quality and to share the emotions of kings. The same goes for style: an aristocracy tends to impose on playwrights certain modes of expression that set the key in which everything must be delivered. In this way the stage often comes to depict only one side of man, or sometimes even to represent what cannot be found in human nature at all, rising above nature and going beyond it.

note: manner and simplicity of manners are social behavior
heading of the book on manners in the narrow sense
Book Three: civility and gentleness of social behavior
caste customs alongside modes of living
replacement: This applies exactly to the subject we are now considering. In an aristocratic community, all men are fixed irrevocably in their places by profession, property, and birth. The members of each class regard themselves as children of one family and feel a constant, lively sympathy for one another, which the citizens of a democracy can never feel to the same degree. But the several classes do not feel the same way toward one another. Among an aristocratic people, each caste has its own opinions, feelings, rights, customs, and ways of living. So the men of each caste do not resemble the mass of their fellow citizens. They do not think or feel in the same way, and they hardly believe that they belong to the same human race. They therefore cannot fully understand what others feel, or judge others by themselves. Yet they are sometimes eager to help one another, and this does not contradict my earlier remark. These aristocratic institutions made beings of one and the same race very different, but they nevertheless tied them to one another by close political bonds. The serf had no natural interest in the fate of nobles, yet he still thought himself obliged to devote his person to the service of whichever noble happened to be his lord. And although the noble considered himself of a different nature from his serfs, he nevertheless held that his duty and his honor required him to defend, at the risk of his own life, those who lived on his lands.
